title: Harry Belafonte: The Real Deal
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Harry Belafonte, the actor, singer, Tony and EGOT winner and civil rights and humanitarian activist, timed to Black History Month. They cover his Jamaican childhood, Navy service, early stage career at the American Negro Theater, and his folk and calypso music, including the hit "Day-O (The Banana Boat Song)" and the 1956 album Calypso. They discuss his refusal to take demeaning Hollywood roles, his civil rights work with Martin Luther King Jr., his Tonight Show guest hosting, his anti-apartheid and famine-relief work including "We Are the World," his late-life prison advocacy, his death in 2023, and his Beetlejuice appearance. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about the Halifax Christmas tree.

segments.title: Opening banter and Black History Month
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the show's anniversary and the We Are the World documentary, then introduce Harry Belafonte as a Black History Month profile.

segments.title: Introducing Harry Belafonte
segments.summary: The hosts describe Belafonte as an entertainer and activist known for Day-O, and explain what an EGOT is.

segments.title: Day-O and the banana boat work song
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Day-O was a call-and-response work song from banana boat dockworkers, where the tally man counted loads before workers could go home.

segments.title: Early life in Harlem, Jamaica, and the Navy
segments.summary: Belafonte was born in Harlem to Caribbean parents, lived in Jamaica from about age eight, was raised by his grandmother there, and joined the Navy in 1944, serving in an all-Black unit in World War II.

segments.title: Marriage to Marguerite Byrd and theater beginnings
segments.summary: Belafonte's first marriage to Marguerite Byrd and his radicalization are discussed. He worked as a janitor's assistant and stage hand at the American Negro Theater, alongside Sidney Poitier, and studied at the New School with classmates including Walter Matthau, Marlon Brando and Tony Curtis.

segments.title: Shift to singing and the folk revival
segments.summary: Unable to find dignified roles, Belafonte turned to singing jazz standards and then folk music, which connected him to the early 1940s Greenwich Village folk revival and performers such as Lead Belly.

segments.title: Research at the Library of Congress and Paul Robeson
segments.summary: Belafonte researched folk songs at the Library of Congress, and he admired Paul Robeson, which led him toward Caribbean calypso folk music. His stage act was a sensation, and he won a Tony in 1954 as the first Black man to win one.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Calypso craze and the Lord Burgess collaboration
segments.summary: Belafonte's calypso success is described, with credit to Lord Burgess (Irving Burgie) and William Attaway for rearranging traditional songs into a more popular form.

segments.title: Calypso purists and the 1956 album
segments.summary: Trinidadian calypso purists criticized Belafonte, and the hosts discuss his 1959 New York Times remarks. His 1956 album Calypso went to number one for 38 weeks and became the first album to sell a million copies in its first year.

segments.title: Racism on the road and in America
segments.summary: Despite his stardom, Belafonte faced segregation: hotels in Las Vegas refused him, he was threatened in a whites-only bathroom while touring the South, and he was stopped by police in Beverly Hills.

segments.title: Island in the Sun and interracial romance on screen
segments.summary: Belafonte took the role in Island in the Sun (1957), which had an implied romance with Joan Fontaine. The South Carolina legislature reportedly moved to ban the film from theaters. His second wife, Julie Robinson, was white.

segments.title: Refusing demeaning roles and Sidney Poitier rivalry
segments.summary: Belafonte turned down roles he called Uncle Tom roles, and rejected Lilies of the Field, which Poitier took and won an Oscar for. The hosts describe the rivalry and friendship with Poitier.

segments.title: Civil rights work with Martin Luther King Jr.
segments.summary: After a phone call from King in 1956 and a four-hour meeting, Belafonte became deeply involved in civil rights. He bailed out activists, helped fund Freedom Rides and Mississippi efforts, co-organized the March on Washington, and supported King's family.

segments.title: Hosting The Tonight Show and TV backlash
segments.summary: In 1968 Johnny Carson had Belafonte guest host The Tonight Show, with guests including Bobby Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. Belafonte's TV specials drew big ratings but sponsors pulled out, and he grew disillusioned with Hollywood.

segments.title: We Are the World and global causes
segments.summary: Belafonte called Quincy Jones to start We Are the World for Ethiopian famine relief, which raised about $65 million. Radio stations worldwide played it simultaneously in 1986. The hosts also cite his work on apartheid and Kenyan independence.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Later career, Emmy, and fatigue of activism
segments.summary: Belafonte became the first Black American to win an Emmy in 1960 for Tonight with Belafonte. He left show business for stretches and returned in the early 1970s to appear in Buck and the Preacher, which Poitier directed. Belafonte described the toll of activism in a testy 1960s-era quote.

segments.title: Paul Robeson as model and blacklisting
segments.summary: The hosts describe Paul Robeson's peace work during the Cold War, his State Department passport suspension from 1950 to 1958, and his blacklisting, which served as a model for Belafonte.

segments.title: Community criticism and personal life
segments.summary: Belafonte was criticized within the Black community for marrying white women, and he said he had few Black people at his concerts. He married Pamela Frank in 2008 after splitting from Julie Robinson in 2004.

segments.title: Later activism, death, and honors
segments.summary: Belafonte pursued causes including Riker's Island concerts, prison advocacy and child incarceration, and peace work between the Crips and Bloods. He died April 25, 2023, at 96. Honors include an EGOT, the Kennedy Center Honor, the National Medal of Arts, and a Harlem library named after him, plus Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2022.
topics: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

segments.title: Beetlejuice and Muppets appearances
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Belafonte's songs in Beetlejuice, including Jump in the Line, which Catherine O'Hara suggested. They also mention his Muppet Show performance of Day-O and his popularity with kids.

segments.title: Closing remarks on Belafonte
segments.summary: The hosts recommend listening to Belafonte's recordings and watching footage of his performances, then move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Halifax Christmas tree
segments.summary: A listener notes that Halifax has sent Boston a Christmas tree every year since the Halifax explosion, as thanks for Boston's help. The hosts discuss pronunciation of the listener's name, Matthias.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to send email and close the episode.
